speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you are having difficulty conceiving and experiencing discomfort during sexual activity; can you describe exactly where you feel pain and when these symptoms started?

speaker: Patient
text: 30-year-old female. The patient and her husband have been trying to conceive for 15 months without success. They are sexually active at least twice a week. The husband occasionally has difficulties maintaining an erection. The patient reports discomfort and pelvic floor muscle tension during attempted vaginal penetration. Diagnosed with body dysmorphic disorder three years ago. No family history of serious illness. She is a non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. No medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is helpful context. Given the pelvic floor muscle tension you described and the pain with penetration, do you experience any pain when you push in on yourself or during a pelvic exam, or is it only during intercourse? Also, are you currently using any lubricants?

speaker: Patient
text: he is a non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. No medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: The patient reports pelvic floor muscle tension and pain only during intercourse, with no pain on self-palpation; are you noticing any vaginal dryness, spotting, or a burning sensation specifically with urination? Please also confirm if the pain is localized to the entrance (introital) or deeper within the pelvis.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Body Dysmorphic Disorder diagnosed three years ago. Social history: Does not smoke or drink alcohol.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Vulvovaginal Vestibulitis (provoked vestibulodynia).

The history of pain limited to the vaginal introit, pelvic floor tension, and lack of pain on self-palpation is classic for this condition. We will proceed with a diagnostic cotton-swab test to confirm the tenderness.
